Extremely Disappointing Service – Loyal Customer Treated Poorly.

I have been a regular customer of Paris Bakery for years and have always purchased cheese  Batasha from here. Unfortunately, my recent experience has been extremely disappointing and unacceptable.

The last batch of Batasha I received was horribly made and completely inedible. I genuinely wanted to return the unopened packet and sent my driver to the shop, but the owner’s brother Behram flatly refused, stating a zero return policy, with absolutely no willingness to listen or understand the issue. All he kept saying is that he is just managing the shop in Danesh’s absence .
And he has no say in anything..
This  is shocking, especially for a long-standing customer.

What is even more frustrating is that when customers visit the shop, the owner is more than happy to offer multiple items to taste and strongly encourage purchases. However, when a customer has a genuine quality complaint and wants to return a defective product, there is zero accountability and zero courtesy.

This kind of one-sided customer service is ridiculous and deeply disappointing.

Quality has clearly gone downhill, and the way loyal clients are treated is unacceptable.
Despite being very fond of their batashas, I can confidently say that I will never step into this shop again.

Paris Bakery has lost a loyal customer due to poor quality and even poorer customer handling.

featured_reviews.name: Fnp Post
featured_reviews.review_text:
From maska khari to milk buns, Paris Bakery’s delicacies are still drawing regulars to its doorstep. A notice mandating a switch to cleaner fuels, however, is threatening its future.

Dukkar Galli’s hugely loved Paris Bakery now worried over pollution curbs

At a time when everyone around him was baking and selling bread, Danish Nejadkay wanted more. So, when he took over Paris Bakery in 1985, he shifted focus to biscuits and baked goods. Over the years, he developed recipes for Shrewsbury biscuits, palmiers, cashew macrons, cheese papdi, walnut oats cookies, cake toast, milk buns, wine biscuits, and cheese sticks—over 20 items in total.

Sold from a modest counter at the front, these treats are made in a larger production unit behind it on Dr Cawasji Hormusji Street, popularly known as Dukkar Galli. Once lined with pork shops catering to the Catholic community, this street in Dhobi Talao, Marine Lines, has been home to the bakery for 70 years.

Nejadkay, 62, shared that Paris Bakery was started by a Parsi family in 1955. “My father entered into a partnership with them in 1963,” he said, adding that his grandfather and father also ran Brabourne Bakery in Chira Bazaar. As for the name Paris Bakery, he suspects that some gentleman went to Paris and named it after being charmed by the French city.

Like any long standing establishment, Paris Bakery has seen its share of drama. In 1975, Nejadkay’s father and his partners handed over the bakery’s management to a Gujarati gentleman. A decade later, when Nejadkay dropped out of engineering college to join the family business, the gentleman refused to return the bakery. “He told us to go to court. We did everything we could and eventually threw him out, telling him to go to court instead,” he recalled. The ‘90s were a golden period for the bakery, but Nejadkay has also faced betrayals. “I have been robbed and cheated by my employees many times. Once, there was even a dacoity at midnight,” he said.

While he speaks, the bakery’s eclectic decor catches the eye—figurines and posters of religious and non-religious gurus fill the space. At the centre stands a brass idol of Ahura Mazda, the supreme god of Zoroastrianism. To the right are images of Mother Teresa, Jesus, a hand-painted Indian goddess, and Buddha. To the left, photos of Paramahansa Yogananda sit beside a Ganesh idol, a Laughing Buddha statue, and a gold-framed portrait of Nejadkay’s father. “I am religious, but for me, religion is like parents. You should respect yours without disrespecting others,” he shared.

The secret sauce: Quality products and Amul butter

There was a time when Paris Bakery operated from 5 am to midnight. Today, it runs from 10 am to 1.30 pm and again from 5 pm to 7.30 pm. On Sundays, it opens for just two and a half hours. Manning the counter is Nejadkay’s brother Behram, a retired Navy merchant.

“You should do everything with heart and soul, and then you won’t have to chase customers—they will come to you,” Nejadkay said. His words ring true. Though there is no visible rush, Behram shares that a queue forms before the shutters rise in the morning and evening.

During our visit, we saw a steady stream of customers. Nejadkay’s clientele includes well-dressed men and women from the neighbourhood, picking up maska khari, maska button, and milk toast. Some even ask when he will make a particular dish. “Whenever I come up with an idea, I develop a recipe and offer it as a free sample. If customers like it, I add it to the menu,” he said.

Certain items, like milk buns, have a niche following. “I make milk buns just once a week, on days when production is lower. They are made with condensed milk and the best raisins—the kind you won’t find even in the city’s best restaurants. Each bun costs Rs 25, and some customers don’t mind waiting up to 10 days for them,” he said.

The secret to his loyal following? “Full butter,” Nejadkay said. “If everyone used full butter, they all would have been a hit.” In the kitchen, large blocks of Amul ghee sit atop mounds of white flour

Timing- 7am to 9pm

featured_reviews.name: Aditya Bharsake
featured_reviews.review_text:
Stepping into Sassanian feels like walking into a time capsule aged tiles, vintage mirrors, and that unmistakable old-world Irani café charm. You can almost picture Bollywood legends sipping chai here once upon a time.

Now let’s talk food;
Mawa Cake: Soft and nostalgic, though slightly underwhelming on flavor. Still, it has that old-school appeal. 3.5/5

Bread Pudding: Sadly didn’t live up to the legacy. A bit too soggy and bland for our taste. 2/5

Caramel Pudding: Smooth and sweet, but lacked that rich, caramel depth. Still a decent pick if you love simple desserts. 3/5

Bhurji Pav: Star of the show! Perfectly spiced, comforting, and a total mood. Highly recommend.

Veg Puff: Stuffing was tasty, but the outer pastry felt oily; could use some refinement. Friend said the chicken puff was "just okay" too.

Spent ₹400 for 2, Value for money considering the ambiance and legacy.

Overall: 3/5
Would I go again? Maybe not for the food, but absolutely for the experience. The café has character, history, and a charm that’s fading in today’s fast-food era. Come for the vibe, order the bhurji pav, soak in the nostalgia, and take a moment to slow down.

People usually visit Yazdani Bakery for their cookies, especially the famous fortune cookies, which are quite popular here.

Overall, it’s a lovely place to experience Mumbai’s old bakery culture and timeless flavors.

featured_reviews.name: Donggeon Kang
featured_reviews.review_text: Yazdani is more about history and vibe than food. The bakery feels frozen in time which is part of its charm. Not fancy, not polished, but a unique Mumbai experience you won’t find elsewhere.

featured_reviews.name: swati geriani
featured_reviews.review_text:

We took fortune cookies and Ginger cookies - go for them if you are looking for less sweet, and sumptuous bakery item.
This place is great reminder of rawness of Mumbai, old shop tucked in streets of Colaba :)

featured_reviews.name: Sourajyoti
featured_reviews.review_text:
Yazdani Bakery is one of those places in Mumbai that feels frozen in time. Started in 1953, it has been run by the same family for generations and still carries the old Irani café charm. The bakery is located in an old heritage building near Fort and Colaba, and the moment you step inside, you feel like you’ve walked into a different era — with its wooden furniture, old photographs, and simple, no-nonsense setup.
Yazdani is best known for its brun maska (soft bun with butter) and Irani chai, which is probably the most popular order here. Their mawa cake is legendary — rich, soft and full of flavour — and often sells out quickly. Other favourites include khari biscuits, apple pie, plum cake, and freshly baked breads and cookies. Everything tastes homemade and fresh, which is what keeps people coming back.
The place is not fancy, and service is simple, but that’s part of its charm. You come here not for luxury, but for nostalgia, honest food, and a slice of old Bombay. If you want to experience Mumbai’s Irani café culture and enjoy some classic bakery items, Yazdani is a must-visit.

featured_reviews.name: Chester Chua
featured_reviews.review_text:
Perhaps I don’t understand the Parsi cuisine, but I really don’t get the deal with bun maska and mawa cake. Bun maska is basically bread with butter. That’s it. The bread isn’t toasted or anything. Just a plain bread roll. The mawa cake is also just a sponge cake.

Not too sure if I was ripped off, but at INR60 and INR45 respectively, this is way more expensive than other snacks that are more interesting, such as a vada pav for just INR25.

Unless you’re a local looking for nostalgia, I suggest giving this a miss.

featured_reviews.name: Sakib Mulla
featured_reviews.review_text:
Yazdani Bakery Takeaway: A Taste of Nostalgia
Yazdani Bakery is more than just a place to grab a bite; it's a living monument to Mumbai’s Irani cafe heritage. Opting for a takeaway from this institution is a smart choice for those eager to savor its legendary bakes without the old-school dine-in experience (currently limited anyway).
The magic lies in the Brun Maska—a crusty, yet tender, bread generously slathered with creamy butter—and the dense, aromatic Mawa Cake. These staples are impeccably fresh, a testament to the bakery's commitment to quality ingredients and traditional wood-fire ovens. Don't overlook the Shrewsbury Biscuits or the flaky, savory Khari. Packaging is basic and efficient—perfectly functional for transport.
While the interior retains a charmingly worn, antique aesthetic, the focus here is the edible legacy. The staff can occasionally be brisk, but the efficiency ensures a quick transaction. A Yazdani takeaway isn't just buying baked goods; it's securing a comforting, consistent piece of culinary history to enjoy in your own space. It's an indispensable, buttery, sweet slice of Mumbai.

featured_reviews.name: Arin Paul
featured_reviews.review_text:
Cafe Markiv’s feels like a café that knows exactly what it wants to be and stays within that comfort zone. It offers a fairly extensive menu of continental and café-style dishes, presented neatly and priced in the mid-range for the area.

We tried the Americano, Peach Iced Tea, Grilled Chicken Risotto, and Chicken Markiv’s.

The Americano was straightforward and clean, no bitterness, no complexity. It does what an Americano is expected to do, without leaving a strong impression either way. The Peach Iced Tea was refreshing and mildly sweet, pleasant enough for Mumbai weather, though not particularly memorable.

The Chicken Risotto was decent. Creamy, adequately cooked, and comforting, but lacked depth or a distinct flavour punch. It felt safe rather than inspired. A good option if you’re in the mood for something mild and filling, but not something you’d crave or remember later.

The Chicken Markiv’s, which appears to be one of their signature dishes, was served well and plated nicely. The chicken was tender and paired with mashed potatoes and vegetables. Again, the flavours were balanced and acceptable, but it didn’t rise above being just fine. Nothing was wrong with the dish, but nothing truly stood out either.

The menu itself is broad, covering pizzas, burgers, pasta, risottos, rice plates, and main course options, both vegetarian and non-vegetarian. It caters well to mixed groups with varied preferences. Portions are reasonable, and pricing is what you’d expect from a café of this type.

Service was polite and timely, without being overly warm or inattentive. The ambience is comfortable and casual, suitable for conversations, short meetings, or a relaxed meal, though it doesn’t have a distinct character that sets it apart from similar cafés.

Overall, Cafe Markiv’s is reliable but unremarkable. Nothing great, nothing bad. It’s a decent place if you’re nearby and want a predictable café meal without surprises. Not a destination café, but functional and consistent for what it offers.

featured_reviews.review_text:
I’d always wanted to visit one of the oldest bakeries in town ,Kyani & Co.and finally got the chance. The ambience is wonderfully nostalgic, filled with old-school charm, and I absolutely loved that part of the experience.

However, the food didn’t quite live up to the hype. The dishes we tried, like the kheema and bhurji, felt quite basic and nothing exceptional. On the brighter side, the snack items were much better , the mawa cake, chicken cutlet, and ,caramel custard were genuinely enjoyable.

Overall, the pricing is reasonable, making it worth a visit for the ambience and certain snacks, but don’t expect too much from the main dishes.

featured_reviews.name: Janhavi Raut
featured_reviews.review_text:
Kyani & Co. is a classic Iranian café serving authentic Iranian cuisine. The place is always crowded, and you’ll notice a good mix of locals and foreigners, which shows how popular and well-known it is.

Coming to the food, their chicken dishes stood out. The Chicken Cheese Kebab was actually very nice—it was stuffed with cheese from inside and had a hot-dog–like shape. It felt filling and had a good amount of chicken, which I liked the most.

I also tried the chicken samosa, but I felt the chicken quantity was a bit less, with more masala in the filling. Similarly, the mutton cutlet had more potato than mutton. Personally, I prefer meat-forward dishes.

The ambience is really great with an old-world charm, but photography is not allowed inside. I clicked one photo and was asked not to take pictures, which was a bit disappointing considering how beautiful the place is.

Overall, it’s an authentic Iranian café with a lovely atmosphere. The food is good, especially the chicken items, though the filling ratios may not suit everyone’s taste.

featured_reviews.name: Viraj Redkar
featured_reviews.review_text:
Visited Kyani & Co. and honestly, it felt less like a café visit and more like a journey back in time. The moment you walk in, the old-world charm hits you — vintage wooden furniture, classic tiled floors, and an atmosphere that carries stories from over 100 years ago. It’s raw, real, and beautifully untouched.
We ordered the iconic Irani chai, bun maska, and kheema pav — and every bite was pure nostalgia. The chai had that perfect strong, comforting flavor, the bun maska was soft with just the right amount of buttery goodness, and the kheema pav was rich, flavorful, and absolutely satisfying.
What makes this place special isn’t just the food — it’s the experience. No fancy frills, no modern distractions, just timeless simplicity done right.
A small heads-up: it’s strictly cash only — no cards, no UPI — which somehow adds to its old-school vibe.
If you’re in Mumbai and want to experience something authentic, soulful, and truly fascinating, this place is not just a café… it’s a legacy you can taste.

Kyani and Co is a classic institution with delicious food that's definitely worth a visit! The Irani chai and bun maska and and the world famous chicken puff was too good the other food options are amazing, just like the old days. However, do keep in mind that parking can be a challenge - no parking facility is available, and roadside parking can be risky with towing a possibility. But if you're willing to take a short walk or plan ahead, the food is definitely worth it. A must-visit for Irani cuisine lovers.
Would love to see a bit more attention to cleanliness and hygiene, though - that would take it to the next level.
